16.4. Validation findings and interpretation¶

1. Accuracy alone is misleading. The majority baseline achieved 57.586% accuracy while predicting every website as legitimate. It missed all 19,917 validation phishing observations; phishing precision, recall and F1 were zero. Balanced accuracy was 0.5. The learned classifiers must therefore be assessed using phishing metrics and error counts, not only improvement in accuracy.

2. Logistic Regression performed strongly on this internal split. Validation accuracy was 99.925%, phishing precision 99.955%, recall 99.869% and F1 99.912%. It produced 9 false alarms and missed 26 phishing observations, for 35 errors out of 46,958 validation records. Training converged without an optimizer warning. A linear decision rule with the recorded predictors already captures substantial separation in this dataset.

3. Random Forest had fewer validation errors. Accuracy was 99.964%, phishing precision 99.995%, recall 99.920% and F1 99.957%. It produced 1 false alarm and missed 16 phishing observations, for 17 total errors. It is the preferred candidate under the previously stated validation F1 rule. The F1 gap is approximately 0.045 percentage points, not evidence of universal or statistically established superiority. Random Forest also required more training time in this run; timings depend on hardware and environment.

4. Error types have different consequences. A false negative leaves a phishing observation undetected, whereas a false positive incorrectly flags a legitimate observation. The fixed threshold was 0.5; no cost-aware threshold study or probability calibration was performed. Predicted probabilities should not be described as calibrated risk estimates.

5. Very high scores require a bounded conclusion. Recorded content features already showed strong class separation in EDA. Unverified measurement details, source selection, possible collection bias, repeated observations and registered-domain/campaign/template dependence remain relevant. Excluding the three uncertain reference scores does not establish that every remaining feature is free of leakage or collection effects. No such claim is made.

6. The test partition remains unscored. Validation was used to compare these fixed candidates. A final test report is a separate next step after the model/threshold decisions are fixed. Earlier exposure to this dataset means even that internal test cannot be presented as new external confirmation. No external or temporal generalization result has been obtained.

17. One controlled feature-reduction experiment¶

17.1. Fixed design and selection data¶

Question: Can a smaller recorded-feature set maintain validation performance under the same Random Forest settings? The original 48-feature model is the reference. No new feature is engineered. No test score is computed.

The candidate set is constructed inside the training partition. A temporary host-grouped 80/20 split of training data is used to fit a selector model and measure permutation importance. Original validation labels are not used to construct the feature ranking or tune the feature count.

Design item Fixed choice
Selector Clone of the original Random Forest pipeline; same classifier settings
Inner split GroupShuffleSplit, 20% of training host groups held out; seed=142
Importance Decrease in phishing F1 after permuting each original column
Importance computation Fixed sample of at most 4000 inner-holdout rows; 3 repeats; seed=42
Dependence screen At most one representative per numeric Spearman component with absolute correlation >=0.90, computed in inner training
Budget At most 20 original predictors; TLD counts as one original predictor
Final comparison Refit the reduced candidate on all original training rows; score original validation only
Selection rule Prefer the reduced candidate only if both validation phishing F1 and recall are no lower than the full model; otherwise retain the full model

Permutation importance is model- and metric-specific. Three repeats and a sampled inner holdout give a noisy diagnostic, not a confidence interval or proof that a zero/negative-importance field is useless. Correlated fields can mask each other's importance. A graph component is a screening heuristic, not proof that its columns are interchangeable. Only one reduced configuration is tested; the budget/threshold will not be adjusted after seeing its validation score. Permutation importance, correlated features.

The baseline and all shuffled scores use the identical fixed inner-holdout sample. Importance uses the same inclusive probability threshold 0.5 as final validation scoring. No internal subsampling is performed during permutation scoring.

from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
REDUCTION=ROOT/'reports/feature_reduction'
REDUCTION.mkdir(parents=True,exist_ok=True)
reduction_before_hash=hashlib.sha256(pd.util.hash_pandas_object(X_train,index=True).values.tobytes()).hexdigest()
feature_budget=20
correlation_screen=.90
inner_groups=academic_metadata.loc[X_train.index,'host_group']
selector_split=GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1,test_size=.20,random_state=142)
inner_fit_pos,inner_review_pos=next(selector_split.split(X_train,groups=inner_groups))
inner_fit_ids=X_train.index[inner_fit_pos];inner_review_ids=X_train.index[inner_review_pos]
assert not set(inner_groups.loc[inner_fit_ids])&set(inner_groups.loc[inner_review_ids])
assert set(inner_fit_ids).isdisjoint(set(X_validation.index))
assert set(inner_review_ids).isdisjoint(set(X_validation.index))
selector_pipeline=clone(fitted_models['Random Forest'])
selector_pipeline.fit(X_train.loc[inner_fit_ids],y_train.loc[inner_fit_ids])
importance_review_X=X_train.loc[inner_review_ids].sample(n=min(4000,len(inner_review_ids)),random_state=SEED)
importance_review_y=y_train.loc[importance_review_X.index]
def threshold_phishing_f1(estimator,features,target):
    positive_index=int(np.flatnonzero(estimator.classes_==1)[0])
    predictions=(estimator.predict_proba(features)[:,positive_index]>=threshold).astype(int)
    return f1_score(target,predictions,zero_division=0)
importance_reference_f1=threshold_phishing_f1(selector_pipeline,importance_review_X,importance_review_y)
importance_result=permutation_importance(selector_pipeline,importance_review_X,
    importance_review_y,scoring=threshold_phishing_f1,n_repeats=3,max_samples=1.0,random_state=SEED,n_jobs=1)
assert set(importance_review_X.index).issubset(set(inner_review_ids))
print('Importance reference F1 on the same fixed sample:',importance_reference_f1)

importance_table=pd.DataFrame({'feature':predictor_columns,
    'mean_F1_decrease':importance_result.importances_mean,
    'repeat_SD':importance_result.importances_std})
importance_table=importance_table.sort_values(['mean_F1_decrease','feature'],ascending=[False,True])
importance_table.to_csv(REDUCTION/'inner_holdout_importance.csv',index=False)
display(importance_table.round(6))
print('Inner fitting rows:',len(inner_fit_ids))
print('Inner review rows:',len(inner_review_ids))
print('The ranking uses training rows only; original validation and test are not used here.')

17.2. Construct one reduced set¶

A graph joins numeric fields whose inner-training absolute Spearman correlation is at least 0.90. The highest ranked field represents each connected component; ties are resolved by feature name. TLD is its own component. The first 20 component representatives in the importance ranking form the candidate. Fields and removal reasons are listed explicitly. A removed field may still contain useful information; the validation comparison tests the candidate as a whole.

inner_correlations=X_train.loc[inner_fit_ids,numeric_columns].corr(method='spearman')
parent={c:c for c in predictor_columns}
def component_root(c):
    while parent[c]!=c:
        parent[c]=parent[parent[c]]
        c=parent[c]
    return c
def join_components(a,b):
    a,b=component_root(a),component_root(b)
    if a!=b:parent[b]=a
screen_pairs=[]
for a,b in combinations(numeric_columns,2):
    rho=inner_correlations.loc[a,b]
    if pd.notna(rho) and abs(rho)>=correlation_screen:
        join_components(a,b)
        screen_pairs.append({'feature_a':a,'feature_b':b,'inner_training_spearman':rho})
pd.DataFrame(screen_pairs,columns=['feature_a','feature_b','inner_training_spearman']).to_csv(REDUCTION/'correlation_screen.csv',index=False)
representatives={}
for c in importance_table.feature:
    representatives.setdefault(component_root(c),c)
ranked_representatives=[c for c in importance_table.feature if representatives[component_root(c)]==c]
chosen_set=set(ranked_representatives[:feature_budget])
reduced_columns=[c for c in predictor_columns if c in chosen_set]
reduced_numeric=[c for c in numeric_columns if c in chosen_set]
reduced_categorical=[c for c in categorical_columns if c in chosen_set]
assert 0<len(reduced_columns)<=feature_budget<len(predictor_columns)
selection_rows=[]
for c in predictor_columns:
    representative=representatives[component_root(c)]
    reason=('Selected component representative within fixed budget' if c in chosen_set else
            'Screened in favor of component representative: '+representative if c!=representative else
            'Below fixed representative budget')
    selection_rows.append({'feature':c,'selected':c in chosen_set,'component_representative':representative,'reason':reason})
feature_selection_table=pd.DataFrame(selection_rows)
feature_selection_table.to_csv(REDUCTION/'selection_decisions.csv',index=False)
with pd.option_context('display.max_rows',None,'display.max_colwidth',100):display(feature_selection_table)
print('Original predictors:',len(predictor_columns))
print('Reduced predictors:',len(reduced_columns))

17.3. Refit and compare the fixed reduced candidate¶

The Random Forest classifier parameters and 0.5 probability threshold remain unchanged. The reduced model's one-hot encoder is fitted anew on the original training rows. Numeric values are not scaled, as in the full tree pipeline. The original validation set and phishing-positive metric definitions are reused. Fit time is descriptive and hardware-dependent. No statistical equivalence claim is inferred from the single validation comparison.

reduced_transformers=[('numeric','passthrough',reduced_numeric)]
if reduced_categorical:
    reduced_transformers.append(('tld',OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore',sparse_output=True,dtype=np.float64),reduced_categorical))
reduced_preprocessor=ColumnTransformer(reduced_transformers,remainder='drop',sparse_threshold=.3)
reduced_rf=Pipeline([('preprocess',reduced_preprocessor),
    ('classifier',clone(fitted_models['Random Forest'].named_steps['classifier']))])
assert reduced_rf.named_steps['classifier'].get_params()==fitted_models['Random Forest'].named_steps['classifier'].get_params()
started=time.perf_counter()
reduced_rf.fit(X_train[reduced_columns],y_train)
reduced_fit_seconds=time.perf_counter()-started
reduced_probability=reduced_rf.predict_proba(X_validation[reduced_columns])[:,int(np.flatnonzero(reduced_rf.classes_==1)[0])]
reduced_prediction=(reduced_probability>=threshold).astype(int)
reduced_cm=confusion_matrix(y_validation,reduced_prediction,labels=[0,1])
tn,fp,fn,tp=reduced_cm.ravel()
reduced_metrics={'Accuracy':accuracy_score(y_validation,reduced_prediction),
    'Precision (phishing)':precision_score(y_validation,reduced_prediction,zero_division=0),
    'Recall (phishing)':recall_score(y_validation,reduced_prediction,zero_division=0),
    'F1 (phishing)':f1_score(y_validation,reduced_prediction,zero_division=0),
    'Balanced accuracy':balanced_accuracy_score(y_validation,reduced_prediction),
    'False alarms (FP)':int(fp),'Missed phishing (FN)':int(fn),
    'Detected phishing (TP)':int(tp),'Correct legitimate (TN)':int(tn),'Fit seconds':reduced_fit_seconds}
full_metrics=validation_metrics.loc['Random Forest'].to_dict()
reduction_comparison=pd.DataFrame([full_metrics,reduced_metrics],index=['Full Random Forest','Reduced Random Forest'])
reduction_comparison['Original predictors']=[len(predictor_columns),len(reduced_columns)]
reduction_comparison['Encoded predictors']=[len(fitted_models['Random Forest'].named_steps['preprocess'].get_feature_names_out()),
                                         len(reduced_rf.named_steps['preprocess'].get_feature_names_out())]
reduction_comparison.to_csv(REDUCTION/'validation_comparison.csv',index_label='Candidate')
display(reduction_comparison.round(6))
select_reduced=(reduced_metrics['F1 (phishing)']>=full_metrics['F1 (phishing)'] and
                reduced_metrics['Recall (phishing)']>=full_metrics['Recall (phishing)'])
preferred_variant='Reduced Random Forest' if select_reduced else 'Full Random Forest'
preferred_predictors=reduced_columns if select_reduced else predictor_columns
preferred_rf=reduced_rf if select_reduced else fitted_models['Random Forest']
reduction_protocol={'feature_budget':feature_budget,'inner_seed':142,'permutation_seed':SEED,
    'permutation_repeats':3,'importance_sample_rows':len(importance_review_X),'importance_reference_f1':importance_reference_f1,'correlation_threshold':correlation_screen,
    'selection_data':'Inner grouped holdout of original training partition only',
    'reduced_columns':reduced_columns,'preferred_variant':preferred_variant,'preferred_columns':preferred_predictors,
    'selection_rule':'Reduced only if validation phishing F1 and recall are both no lower; otherwise full',

Decision: Reduced Random Forest is retained under the fixed validation rule. The candidate used 20 original predictors instead of 48. Feature removal is an empirical experiment, not proof of redundancy. No test score was used and no post-result search over feature counts was performed.

17.4. Findings and interpretation¶

1. The single reduced candidate maintained and slightly improved validation F1. Full RF: F1 99.9573%, recall 99.9197%, accuracy 99.9638%. Reduced RF: F1 99.9799%, recall 99.9749%, accuracy 99.9830%. The F1 difference is about 0.0226 percentage points; this is a small internal validation difference, not a statistically established advantage or a guarantee on new data.

2. The error trade-off matters. The full model missed 16 phishing records and falsely flagged 1 legitimate record (17 errors). The reduced model missed 5 phishing records and falsely flagged 3 legitimate records (8 errors). Recall improved but precision declined slightly. Therefore it is incorrect to claim that every metric or error type improved. The predeclared rule used F1 and recall; it selects the reduced candidate on this validation set.

3. Original predictors decreased from 48 to 20; encoded columns from 641 to 20. TLD was not retained by the training-only selection procedure, so the reduced candidate has no one-hot categorical block. These are two different counts: an original categorical variable can expand to many columns. No new predictor was engineered and no feature was removed solely because its name looked suspicious or its zeros were frequent.

4. The ranking and screening do not prove universal redundancy. IsHTTPS, LineOfCode, NoOfSelfRef, HasSocialNet and NoOfSubDomain were among the highest permutation-ranked fields in the fixed inner holdout sample. The recorded IsHTTPS measurement caveat remains applicable. Some selected fields have zero or small measured importance; the fixed 20-field budget is an experimental constraint, not a claim that exactly 20 fields are optimal. Correlated features can substitute for each other, and only three repeats were used. Removed fields may be useful under another model or sample.

5. The comparison keeps parameter values fixed, not every effective tree property. Random Forest's default sqrt feature sampling depends on encoded dimension, so the number of candidate features per split changes when the input shrinks. Reduced training time and error changes cannot be attributed to an isolated feature effect. In this run fitting was roughly 20 seconds for the full model and 8 seconds for the reduced model; timings are contextual.

6. Decision and next boundary. The preferred RF variant is the reduced 20-feature candidate under the stated validation rule. The full comparison and all exclusion reasons remain in the notebook. No test scores were used. The next step is to record the final feature/model/threshold configuration before a separate final test evaluation. Prior dataset exposure and the measurement, collection-bias and host-grouping limits remain unchanged.

18. Frozen final evaluation and internal test results¶

18.1. Protocol recorded before test scoring¶

Primary candidate: Reduced Random Forest with the 20 recorded predictors selected in Section 17. Classifier: 200 trees, max_depth=20, min_samples_leaf=2, random_state=42. Positive class: phishing=1. Probability threshold: 0.5. All models remain fitted on the original training partition; no training-plus-validation refit is performed.

The exact predictor order, estimator parameters, data/split hashes and software versions are recorded in reports/final_evaluation/frozen_protocol.json before this section scores test data. Existing protocol contents must match; they are not overwritten to accommodate a different feature set after evaluation.

Comparisons: Majority baseline, Logistic Regression (48 original fields), Full Random Forest (48), and Reduced Random Forest (20). The full LR/RF pair compares model families with the same inputs; full/reduced RF compares two feature configurations. These are distinct comparisons. The primary choice will not change if the test ordering differs.

The internal test contains 47,583 recorded observations. Prior exposure to this dataset is acknowledged; this is not newly collected external confirmation. No threshold, hyperparameter or feature search is performed in this section.

18.2. Test metrics at the fixed threshold¶

Predictions and probabilities are generated with the already fitted pipelines. The target remains separate from X. Accuracy, phishing precision/recall/F1, balanced accuracy, ROC-AUC, average precision and confusion counts are reported. ROC-AUC and average precision summarize ranking, not probability calibration. No model is selected using these test scores.

test_predictions={};test_probabilities={};test_confusions={};test_rows=[]
for name,model in test_candidates.items():
    test_input=(np.zeros((len(X_test),1)) if name=='Majority baseline' else
                X_test[reduced_columns] if name=='Reduced Random Forest' else X_test)
    positive_index=int(np.flatnonzero(model.classes_==1)[0])
    probability=model.predict_proba(test_input)[:,positive_index]
    assert np.isfinite(probability).all() and ((probability>=0)&(probability<=1)).all()
    prediction=(probability>=threshold).astype(int)
    test_probabilities[name]=probability;test_predictions[name]=prediction
    cm=confusion_matrix(y_test,prediction,labels=[0,1])
    tn,fp,fn,tp=cm.ravel()
    test_confusions[name]=cm
    assert cm.sum()==len(y_test)
    test_rows.append({'Model':name,'Original predictors':0 if name=='Majority baseline' else 20 if name=='Reduced Random Forest' else 48,
        'Accuracy':accuracy_score(y_test,prediction),
        'Precision (phishing)':precision_score(y_test,prediction,zero_division=0),
        'Recall (phishing)':recall_score(y_test,prediction,zero_division=0),
        'F1 (phishing)':f1_score(y_test,prediction,zero_division=0),
        'Balanced accuracy':balanced_accuracy_score(y_test,prediction),
        'ROC-AUC':roc_auc_score(y_test,probability),'Average precision':average_precision_score(y_test,probability),
        'False alarms (FP)':int(fp),'Missed phishing (FN)':int(fn),
        'Detected phishing (TP)':int(tp),'Correct legitimate (TN)':int(tn)})
test_metrics=pd.DataFrame(test_rows).set_index('Model')
test_metrics.to_csv(FINAL/'test_metrics.csv',index_label='Model')
display(test_metrics.round(6))

18.3. Confusion matrices, ranking curves and error records¶

Matrix rows are true classes; columns are predicted classes. False negatives are phishing predicted legitimate, and false positives are legitimate predicted phishing. Curves use phishing as the positive class. Row-level error records are saved locally by source index, without publishing raw URL/query values.

18.5. Final internal test findings¶

1. The frozen primary candidate retained strong internal performance. The 20-predictor Random Forest correctly classified 47,578 of 47,583 test observations. Accuracy was 99.9895%, phishing precision 99.9903%, recall 99.9854% and F1 99.9878%. There were 2 false positives and 3 false negatives. These are counts and metrics for this recorded internal test, not evidence of equivalent performance on an external or future dataset.

2. The majority baseline illustrates why accuracy is insufficient. It achieved 56.7892% accuracy by predicting every observation as legitimate, while missing all 20,561 phishing observations. Its phishing F1 was zero. The test contains 27,022 legitimate observations; class counts and confusion totals are consistent with the 47,583-row partition.

3. The full-feature model ordering changed. With the same 48 original predictors, Logistic Regression obtained F1 99.9562% (10 false alarms, 8 missed phishing observations), whereas full Random Forest obtained 99.9513% (0 false alarms, 20 missed phishing observations). Full RF had slightly higher ranking metrics but lower recall at the fixed 0.5 threshold. Different metrics emphasize different trade-offs; these small differences do not establish statistical or universal superiority of either model.

4. The reduced RF choice was made before this test. Its validation F1 was 99.9799%, compared with test F1 99.9878%; the difference is about +0.0079 percentage points. This does not imply that the test was easier by design or that selection was optimized for it. The original feature set, threshold and classifier settings matched the saved pre-test protocol. No training-plus-validation refit or post-test tuning occurred.

5. Fewer test errors do not prove that removed fields are intrinsically useless. Feature ranking used an inner training holdout and a fixed budget, and only one reduced configuration was evaluated. Sampling, correlated predictors and the forest's dimension-dependent sqrt feature sampling can affect the comparison. The selected subset is a justified experimental configuration, not a universal optimal feature set.

6. Research-question answer and remaining limits. Under the stated recorded-data protocol, URL and webpage measurements support very strong internal class separation, and the selected reduced RF has low measured FP/FN counts. Measurement uncertainty, collection/source bias, repeated observations and possible registered-domain/campaign/template dependence remain. Prior dataset exposure is acknowledged. No causal, probability- calibration or external-generalization claim follows from the scores.

The next reporting tasks are the final English conclusion/evaluation, ethical considerations, consolidated references and the required standalone submission notebook, PDF report, dataset and README package.

19. Conclusion and evaluation¶

19.1. Answer to the research question¶

Research question: How effectively can recorded URL and webpage features distinguish phishing websites from legitimate websites?

The recorded PhiUSIIL features supported very strong internal classification under the stated observed-host-grouped protocol. The frozen primary candidate, a Random Forest using 20 selected recorded predictors, achieved 99.9895% accuracy, 99.9903% phishing precision, 99.9854% phishing recall and 99.9878% phishing F1 on 47,583 test observations. It missed 3 phishing observations and incorrectly flagged 2 legitimate observations. This answers the question for this dataset and experimental protocol, not for all websites or future data.

19.2. What the analysis and comparisons established¶

The source contained 235,795 observations and 56 columns. Missing-value, duplicate, parsing and measurement audits were completed before detailed training-data EDA. Exact URL repetition was distinguished from identical-row duplication. Recorded observations were retained in this academic experiment, and identical observed hosts were kept within one partition. Dataset source and label attribution follow [1] and the associated study metadata [2].

The first predictor schema contained 47 numeric fields and categorical TLD. Identifiers, raw title text and three reference-based scores of uncertain provenance were excluded from the primary experiment. One-hot encoding and numeric scaling, where appropriate, were learned only from training data. The majority baseline demonstrated that accuracy alone can be misleading: it reached 56.7892% test accuracy while detecting no phishing observations.

The full 48-field Logistic Regression and Random Forest were compared with the same inputs. Their test phishing F1 scores were 99.9562% and 99.9513%, respectively. This ordering differed from validation, reinforcing that a small internal gap is not evidence of universal algorithmic superiority.

A single controlled reduction experiment used permutation importance on an inner training holdout and a training-only correlation screen. The selected 20-field candidate was chosen before final test scoring because validation F1 and recall did not decrease. It also produced fewer test errors than the full RF in this run. The result supports the usefulness of a smaller experimental configuration; it does not establish that exactly 20 fields are optimal or that excluded fields are intrinsically useless [12,13].

19.3. Interpretation of the exploratory hypothesis¶

The hypothesis concerned recorded URLLength distributions. With one label-independently selected observation per training hostname, the empirical KS distance was D=0.3783. The 1,999-permutation p estimate was 0.0005, the minimum reportable Monte Carlo value. No permuted statistic was as extreme as observed; the estimate is not an exact population p-value. Under the stated exchangeability assumptions, H₀ was rejected at α=0.05. The representative sample medians were 26 for legitimate and 32 for phishing observations, with a signed rank effect of approximately 0.401 [14,15].

The hypothesis was specified after examining the data, and observed hostnames may still share campaigns or registered domains. The conclusion is therefore exploratory. A distribution difference does not establish causality or show that length alone is sufficient for classification. The original length measurement discrepancy remains a limitation.

19.4. Limitations and further research¶

The very high scores must be interpreted alongside uncertain feature formulas, possible collection/source bias, repeated observations, and strong class separation in recorded page-content measurements. Excluding uncertain reference scores does not prove that all remaining predictors are free of indirect leakage or source effects. The author's public notebooks provide partial method evidence, not verified parity for every supplied value [3–5].

Observed-host grouping does not ensure registered-domain, campaign, template or temporal independence. Earlier experiments exposed this dataset, so the final internal test is not newly obtained external confirmation. Confidence intervals and repeated grouped model evaluation were not performed; differences between the reported candidate scores are descriptive. Threshold 0.5 remained fixed and probabilities were not calibrated.

Useful follow-up work includes feature-provenance verification, registered- domain/campaign audits, repeated grouped evaluation with feature selection inside each training fold, and a separately collected temporal or external dataset. Such follow-up should form a new evaluation rather than tune the current model to the already observed test errors [7,8].

Overall evaluation: The project demonstrates a reproducible recorded-data study connecting quality audits, EDA, justified preprocessing, an exploratory hypothesis, classifier comparison and a limited reduction experiment. Its strongest conclusion is high internal separability under the documented protocol; broader generalization remains unestablished.

20. Ethical considerations and responsible interpretation¶

20.1. Dataset attribution and permitted reuse¶

The dataset is attributed to Arvind Prasad and Shalini Chandra and the UCI Machine Learning Repository. PhiUSIIL is supplied under CC BY 4.0; attribution and a link to the source/license should accompany redistributed data [1]. Derived features, target recoding and subset decisions are distinguished from the unchanged source. The associated paper is cited for dataset attribution; unavailable full-text material is not presented as if it had been verified [2].

20.2. Privacy and safe treatment of recorded addresses¶

Recorded URLs may contain personal identifiers, tokens or sensitive query values, even when the dataset is publicly available. Public availability alone does not justify exposing unnecessary details. Figures and summary tables avoid raw query values, and error records use source-row identifiers. Any raw-data submission should follow the course's permitted submission route and preserve attribution. Sanitized examples should be used in presentation slides when individual records need illustration.

The study analyses the local dataset without visiting suspicious addresses or collecting additional website content. Recorded labels are used as supplied; they are not a new verification of each site's present ownership, content or status.

20.3. Error consequences and bias¶

False negatives represent missed phishing observations, while false positives incorrectly flag legitimate observations. Both matter; selecting a high-accuracy model without discussing phishing recall or false alarms would conceal relevant costs. The final model's three false negatives and two false positives are reported explicitly rather than hidden behind rounded percentages.

Sample composition and recorded page-content differences can favor some sources or website types. TLD association in this sample is not evidence that every website with an extension is suspicious. No broad judgment about a country, organization or domain owner follows from a category-level result. Changes in class prevalence can also change precision outside the sample.

20.4. Research integrity and reproducibility¶

The hypothesis's post-EDA exploratory status, prior dataset exposure, uncertain measurement definitions and incomplete independence are disclosed. A weak baseline, fixed model settings, selected/removed fields, failed assumptions and FP/FN counts are documented. No test-driven feature or threshold adjustment was performed after the final protocol was recorded.

Model-specific importance is not presented as causal importance, a prediction score is not presented as calibrated certainty, and internal test success is not presented as external validation. Dataset, software and inspected feature examples are attributed in the consolidated references. Group members should understand and be able to explain the analysis, decisions and limitations.
